item.title: In L.A., a Stark Generational Divide May Determine the Mayor’s Race
item.description:
Saturday nights usually aren’t prime time for campaigning in Los Angeles elections. Still, there was Nithya Raman, stumping for mayor at a party at a Hollywood art gallery at 9 p.m. on a recent weekend.

Pink lights glowed. Pop tracks bumped. Gen Z influencers posed in a floral garland for Instagram and TikTok. If anyone in the house was a homeowner over 50, they didn’t look it.

“What is happening in Los Angeles is a generational election,” Ms. Raman, 45, said. In the audience, Sable Minx, a 28-year-old social media creator, applauded.

“I work, I would say, three jobs,” she said, “and I still can’t afford to, you know, live on my own, have my own space.” New leadership? That “resonated,” she said.

Though not with everyone.

The next morning Alton Reed, 80, headed out with his wife and a fistful of fliers to walk precincts for Mayor Karen Bass, the 73-year-old incumbent. “That’s the attitude of all young people, isn’t it,” he said, as he walked with a crowd of supporters. “‘Time for a change.’ Whether it’s warranted or not.”

That tension has underpinned the choice facing Los Angeles voters as they decide whether to keep their mayor or elect a new one. From policy proposals to celebrity endorsements, the most consistent subtext has been the age-based divide that has emerged in the nationally watched campaign.

Polls have consistently shown voters under 40 flocking to Ms. Raman, who has been backed by the democratic socialist movement that helped elect New York’s 35-year-old mayor, Zohran Mamdani. Voters over 65 have mostly stood by Ms. Bass, a former state lawmaker and member of Congress and a veteran Democrat.

The split echoes broader trends: Over the past two years, according to a New York Times/Siena University poll, young voters have swung dramatically to the view that the country is on the wrong track, a determination that, in this election at least, has yanked them leftward.

It has also prompted more young people to run for office. Future Caucus, a nonpartisan nonprofit that works with younger elected officials, reported this month that more than a third of this year’s congressional candidates were millennials or Gen Z, a new high for candidates under 45.

In Los Angeles, the margins have been stark, particularly among younger voters. In a survey conducted earlier this month for The Los Angeles Times by the Institute of Governmental Studies at the University of California, Berkeley, 69 percent of likely voters under 30 favored Ms. Raman, as did 74 percent of voters aged 30 to 39.

“Even more than with Mamdani, this is a campaign about generations,” said Dan Schnur, a former Republican political consultant who now teaches political communications at several universities in California.

On one side, he said, are longtime residents who respect the mayor’s deep experience and consider complaints about the current state of Los Angeles in the context of the chaotic city they once knew — a smog-clouded sprawl of racism, rioting, gang crime and police abuses that changed, in large measure, because of people like Ms. Bass. She’s an adult, they say, and this is no time to elect an untested leader, with two more years of the Trump administration and with the Summer Olympics coming in less than two years.

On the other side are waves of new voters who say they have been failed by the leadership of Ms. Bass and her generation. Many newcomers say the gritty city they’ve found doesn’t live up to its billing, and natives wonder what happened to the Southern California where single-family homes and single-occupancy cars were an affordable birthright.

“Think about what that generation has experienced — 9/11, the Great Recession, the #MeToo movement, Covid,” Mr. Schnur said of young voters. “It’s no wonder they’re searching for dramatic change.”

The schism is directly tied to affordability challenges like home prices and other markers of adulthood, which have increasingly moved out of reach for residents under 40. Young residents shoulder an average rent that, at $2,662, is more than 33 percent higher than the national average, according to Zillow. The average homeowner, according to an analysis of census data released last year, is older in Los Angeles than in any other big city in the nation — almost 55.

That calculus already has shifted the city’s conventional political wisdom. Since the early 1970s, when white, Black, Latino and Jewish liberals joined forces to elect the city’s first Black mayor, Tom Bradley, elections in the sprawling city have swung chiefly on the ability to assemble a coalition from socioeconomic and ethnic factions. This year, analysts say, there’s a new cohort.

“This is the first campaign I can recall where age was as significant a factor as racial demography,” said Jim Newton, a former head of the editorial page of The Los Angeles Times and lecturer on public policy at the University of California, Los Angeles.

Michael Rodriguez-Chen, 33, and his wife, Paula Rodriguez-Chen, 32, for example, say they will vote for Ms. Raman. Watching their 3-year-old son dart around a playground in the city’s Eagle Rock neighborhood, they ticked off an assortment of municipal complaints: deteriorating streets, sidewalks turned into mountain ranges by overgrown tree roots.

But what really stood out, Mr. Rodriguez-Chen said, was Ms. Raman’s promise to make housing more affordable by encouraging more apartment construction and establishing tenant protections.

The Rodriguez-Chens work from their two-bedroom, two-bathroom apartment not far from the playground. It’s a little cramped, but at $3,300 per month, it was a good deal. Similar places in their price range would have required them to choose: “Like, do we keep our couch or our table?” recalled Ms. Rodriguez-Chen wryly.

But how long will they stay there? The couple said they didn’t feel they had much choice.

“I don’t know if we’re able to currently move forward,” Mr. Rodriguez-Chen said.

That experience is a far cry from that of Inja Lee, 84, a retiree in the city’s Koreatown district who showed up with scores of Korean American seniors at a recent meet-and-greet with the mayor. Ms. Lee said she appreciated Ms. Bass’s efforts to address homelessness and public safety concerns.

Her experience in Los Angeles dates to the tumultuous 1990s, a decade convulsed by the Los Angeles riots, the Northridge earthquakes and the trial of O.J. Simpson. The proprietor of a greeting card store in nearby Burbank for several decades, she now lives in a Koreatown senior housing complex.

The mayor seemed to understand Los Angeles, she said. “She moved the homeless people to a good place,” Ms. Lee said. “She’s a nice lady. And we know her.”

That split screen extends in ways large and small across the two campaigns. Gen X and millennial stars like Natalie Portman and Poppy Liu dominate Ms. Raman’s list of celebrity supporters. Ms. Bass’s roster reads like a who’s who of silver Angelenos: Jane Fonda, Magic Johnson, Samuel L. Jackson.

Ms. Raman has support from the Los Angeles chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America and most of the transit enthusiasts and lobbies. Ms. Bass has the business establishment, most of the major City Hall unions, the police and every member of the City Council except for Ms. Raman.

Ms. Raman’s campaign has been heavily online, with social media posts featuring influencers and spoofs of microdramas. Ms. Bass’s supporters have papered the city with old-school handouts and door hangers. (The mayor, Mr. Schnur observed with a chuckle, “is running an almost perfect 20th-century campaign.”)

“I’m saddened by it,” Ms. Bass said of the generational divide, pointing to her years as a student activist, her work as a young physician assistant organizing against the 1980s crack epidemic and her mentorship of young Black and Latino leaders at the nonprofit she founded, Community Coalition. If re-elected, she said, her administration will give young people a bigger role.

“But I also understand it, because I was one of those young leaders once,” she said in an interview. “And I was very disgruntled and very dissatisfied and very angry at the status quo.”

The raw numbers would seem to favor Team Raman: almost 57 percent of the city’s electorate is under 50. But turnout is notoriously unpredictable among younger voters. As of Saturday, only 8 percent of Los Angeles voters under 35 had returned their ballots, compared with 31 percent of voters over 65, according to the California-based research firm Political Data Intelligence.

“Now, young people, historically, have not voted in municipal elections,” Ms. Raman called out to her supporters. “Are we going to make our voices heard this time?”

item.title: A Midterm Campaign Dominated by Concerns Over High Prices Nears Its End
item.description:
Financial concerns have been the most pressing issue for voters in four of the six previous midterm elections of this century. But with the war in Iran and tariffs driving up gas prices, inflation and mortgage rates, the worries feel deeper, more desperate and decidedly center stage in the final days of the hard-fought campaign that will decide control of Congress.

Democrats are hammering President Trump for starting a war with Iran and instituting tariffs that have driven up prices, while Republicans are insisting the fundamentals of the economy are stronger than before they took power two years ago. And polls show that pocketbook issues are once again top of mind for many voters.

If presidential elections are about a vision for the future, midterms give voters a chance to offer their verdict on a president, a Congress and, almost always, the nation’s economic health.

Over dozens of interviews across the country in recent days, Americans from across the political spectrum detailed the financial gymnastics of keeping pace with rent hikes and mounting utility bills, along with rising prices for gas, groceries and even Halloween candy. Many voters directly blamed Mr. Trump and his party for the high cost of living.

“The prices of everything we normally buy have gone up and up dramatically,” said Dwayne Stanford, a father of eight in suburban Cincinnati, who chose only Democratic candidates during early voting in his state. “It’s just the everyday stuff.”

“Everybody’s feeling it in terms of inflation,” said Bret Rhodus, 52, an independent voter from Douglas County, Kan. “College costs, because I’m kind of in that stage of life. But even, like, the price of a pizza.”

“It’s expensive,” said Sophia Gallerani, 80, a retiree who said she cast her ballot for the Republican ticket on the first day of early voting in Tucson, Ariz. “Basic needs like eating and gas for getting to appointments if I have any or going to church.”

The worries of voters, which cross lines of generation and gender, race and political ideology, reflect the anxieties of a country convinced that the American dream is slipping away. In polls, focus groups and interviews, voters described some of the traditional promises of a middle-class life — health care, a college education, homeownership and retirement — as becoming rapidly unaffordable. They fear their children will live a worse life than they do.

“I have a degree, I have a good job, but it is still a stretch to pay for basics like groceries and utilities,” said Brandi Kelly, 43, of Dayton, Ohio. “It is harder to just maintain what we have had.”

Presidents often shoulder the blame — and occasionally the credit — for an American economy that they have limited ability to directly control. But Douglas Holtz-Eakin, the former chief economist for President George W. Bush’s Council of Economic Advisers and current president of the conservative American Action Forum, said that old political maxim doesn’t totally apply when it comes to Mr. Trump and some of the signature policies of his administration.

The war with Iran raised gas prices, and tariffs made foreign goods more expensive for U.S. purchasers. The rising costs have outpaced workers’ hourly wages, according to the government, compounding the financial stress already felt by many American families.

“The standard of living is declining and people know that,” Mr. Holtz-Eakin said. “The nature of these actions have really allowed voters to blame him.”

Democrats have driven a message of blaming Mr. Trump for the high costs. Expanding on a theme of “affordability” that the party rode to success in the races for governor in 2025, Democratic candidates and their allies have spent nearly a half-billion dollars on ads mentioning the economy, prices and inflation, according to AdImpact.

In Maine, Troy Jackson, the Democratic Senate nominee, has transformed surging heating oil costs into a central line of attack against Senator Susan Collins, the Republican incumbent.

In North Carolina, former Gov. Roy Cooper, the Democratic Senate nominee, has spent weeks on a “Make Stuff Cost Less” campaign tour, introducing plans to lower the price of food, health care, utilities, child care and housing.

And in Texas, supporters of Gina Hinojosa, the Democratic nominee for governor, wave money-green signs with one of her central campaign promises: “Money in your pocket.”

Even in races dominated by questions of character and corruption, Democrats have steadfastly returned to high costs as the central building block of their political argument.

“We can’t afford the basics in this economy — gas, groceries, utilities, health care — because the system has been rigged by billionaires and crooked politicians like Ken Paxton,” James Talarico, the Democratic Senate nominee in Texas, told a cheering crowd at the Kay Bailey Hutchison Convention Center in Dallas on Thursday evening, referring to his Republican opponent. “This election is about whether you want a senator who puts money in your pocket or money in their own.”

As he crisscrosses the country on a whirlwind campaign tour, Mr. Trump has tried to argue that the economy is strong, growing and rife with new investment. Markets are riding high, consumers are continuing to spend and gross domestic product is increasing, according to recent measures.

But as Mr. Trump’s predecessor, former President Joseph R. Biden Jr., learned during his term in office, voters don’t care how government reports assess the economy. They care how it feels.

“The problem is that the one metric people use to judge the economy is gas prices,” said Steve Moore, a conservative economist who advised Mr. Trump’s first presidential campaign. “You see it wherever you go, with a big sign.”

Some of Mr. Trump’s most devoted supporters continue to profess their loyalty, even as they describe enduring economic pain.

Brenda Pruitt, a three-time voter for Mr. Trump, said she had spent more than $100 on gasoline to drive to Ohio from Kentucky to see the president and other Republican candidates speak at a rally in Chillicothe, Ohio, on Wednesday,

“I’m feeling the inflation, but I’m willing to take less in order to help the American people,” Ms. Pruitt said.

At the rally, Mr. Trump touted the performance of the stock market and higher incomes while blaming Democrats for voting for policies that led to higher prices.

“They voted in favor of the worst inflation and highest energy costs in American history,” Mr. Trump said.

That’s an argument Mr. Trump spent much of 2024 making. More than any other issue, his rise into the White House was fueled by attacks on Mr. Biden and Vice President Kamala Harris for high inflation and promises to lower soaring prices.

Two years later, with inflation rising once again, large numbers of voters have shifted blame to Mr. Trump. Views of his handling of the economy — one of his biggest strengths when he ran on two years ago — are now underwater. Majorities disapprove of his handling of tariffs, the economy, gas prices, the cost of living and the Iran war. Fifty-three percent of likely voters considered the economy as “poor,” in the recent New York Times/Siena poll — the worst rating since July 2022.

Mr. Trump promised to lower inflation; it’s now accelerated to 3.7 percent. He vowed mortgage rates would return to as low as 2 percent. They are currently above 7 percent. And surging fuel prices have increased the costs for farmers, truckers and consumers to heat their homes, plow their fields and commute to work.

Republican efforts to defend the president’s policies, despite growing anger from voters, have fueled Democratic optimism in some surprising places. A clip posted in February of Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, a Republican from Mississippi, responding to concerns about rising beef prices by saying consumers “have so many proteins to choose from,” helped transform her race in a deep red state into a competitive contest.

Her opponent, Scott Colom, has gained ground with a simple slogan: “High wages, lower costs, save our health care.”

In Kansas, Senator Roger Marshall, a Republican, was slow to respond to the rising costs of fertilizer, fuel and feed that have hammered farmers and ranchers in his agriculture-heavy state. The race, which was not on either party’s list of battleground states last year, is now considered one of the most competitive in the country.

“This is one of the best economies I’ve ever seen in my lifetime,” Mr. Marshall said at a campaign stop last month. “We just have to get the price of gas and groceries down.”

The White House has tried to find ways to offer consumers some relief, announcing a series of policies in the final weeks of the campaign that included $90 payouts for millions of seniors on Medicare, $500 rebate checks for some Affordable Care Act customers and a decision to allow Russian diesel imports after years of sanctions.

Mr. Trump has also promised a $5,000 check to every American adult if his party retains control of Congress in November. The plan would require congressional approval and cost more than $1 trillion.

But for many people, such policies are coming too late to affect their finances — or their votes.

As Carmen Moreno, 50, waited to hear Mr. Talarico address the crowd in Dallas, she expressed astonishment at the increase in the cost of food. A recent trip to Denny’s with her mother cost $63, she said.

Ms. Moreno, an entrepreneur, is hopeful Mr. Talarico and a Democratic-controlled Congress can help restore an American middle class that she worries is slipping away.

“We are living in a time with a lot of economic distress,” she said. “And there’s just a total lack of accountably in Congress right now. Like, what is going on?”

Kevin Williams contributed reporting from Butler County, Ohio, Ilana Arougheti from Douglas County, Kan., and Lourdes Medrano from Tucson, Ariz.

item.title: What to Know About ‘Take Back the Night’ Rallies
item.description:
For decades, Take Back the Night, an international organization that has spoken out about sexual violence, has rallied on college campuses across the country and protested around the world.

Active as a grass-roots coalition since the 1970s, the organization has used marches, rallies, protests and speak-outs to push for an end to sexual violence in all forms.

One of the earliest known marches came in 1972, when women at the University of South Florida took up witches’ brooms and donned black capes as they marched across campus using the phrase “take back the night” to demand more resources and increased safety for women.

More than five decades later, sexual violence continues to be a problem on college campuses. The most recent high-profile example occurred at Cornell University, where a woman sued the school and fraternity members there whom she said had sexually assaulted her.

On Sunday, students across more than 90 campuses are expected to march in solidarity with the woman and push to end sexual violence.

Here’s what to know.

The movement began as a loose coalition of groups organizing protests and marches in the 1970s. In 2001, Katie Koestner officially founded the organization Take Back The Night.

Some of the earliest protests by the movement rallied for the safety of women. In 1973, supporters of the movement in San Francisco protested violent “snuff” pornography films. In 1976, women from more than 40 countries came together in Belgium to call for safer streets for women.

In subsequent decades, hundreds of colleges and universities across North America held candlelight vigils, chapel speak-outs and rallies and marches.

At one march at Dartmouth College, protesters stopped in front of fraternity houses where rapes had been reported and dripped candle wax in honor of the survivors who were assaulted there, said Ms. Koestner, the executive director of Take Back the Night.

It was one of dozens of Take Back The Night events Ms. Koestner spoke at after she came out publicly at the age of 18 about being a survivor of date rape on her college campus.

Her case led universities to rethink what they understood to be the definition of rape in the 1990s, she said. Rather than a crime of resistance by the victim and force by the perpetrator, it became a crime of consent, she said.

There has been a particular focus on sexual assault prevention in recent weeks, after a woman’s lawsuit against Cornell University in upstate New York and fraternity members there whom she said had sexually assaulted her in their fraternity house in 2024.

The men have denied that the claims, and none of have been criminally charged. But the woman’s lawsuit brought a flood of criticism to the Ivy League university over how it handled the accusations — two of the men were expelled while others were later allowed to return to campus — as well as the broader handling of sexual assault on and off college campuses.

Ahead of the Sunday rally, Take Back The Night is selling merchandise saying “I am Jane Doe,” in an effort to stand with the anonymous woman who filed the lawsuit.

Earlier this month, a 21-year-old woman also reported that she had been sexually assaulted at a fraternity house near the University of Chicago.

“Every single student should be able to go to college and not be worried about their sexual safety,” Ms. Koestner said in an interview.

Take Back the Night’s virtual rally programming will feature several speakers. Each campus that participates is asked to read five mandates aloud. That includes Cornell University, whose students are holding their march at a local church.

The mandates are directed at the trustees, presidents and administrators of colleges and universities across the United States.

They include calls for:

Evidence-based prevention education for every student.

Trauma-informed investigations and independent oversight.

A 24-hour emergency response and protection for those seeking help.

Monthly public reporting and transparency on campus sexual violence.

The modernization of outdated sexual assault laws.

The organization also provides legal assistance through their hotline, 567-742-8837.

item.title: Did the Peltola Campaign Seal the Fate of Alaska’s Ranked Choice Vote?
item.description:
Organizers of a ballot measure that would end Alaska’s ranked-choice voting system say the effort by Democrats to boost Mary Peltola’s Senate bid by stacking Tuesday’s ballots in an attempt to confuse voters should be the system’s death knell.

Since Alaska voters approved open primaries and ranked-choice general elections in 2020, opponents — most of them Republicans — have argued the system is too confusing for the average person.Now it’s been tainted by scandal involving the recruitment of a challenger with the same name as the incumbent. That has led to federal legal action, a Justice Department investigation and a separate state investigation.

There have been similar attempts to fool the electorate with same-name candidates under other election systems in Alaska and elsewhere.

“I mean, there it is,” said Judy Eledge, a longtime conservative activist in Alaska and chairwoman of the campaign for Ballot Measure 2, the effort to repeal Alaska’s current electoral system that voters will decide next week alongside the race for U.S. Senate. “They’ve done our work for us.”

A similar referendum two years ago lost by 737 votes. Backers of the system still say it encourages bipartisanship and gives voters an extra layer of protection against dirty tricks and bogus candidates by offering multiple choices.

“This situation is actually an object lesson in why you need ranked choice voting: You can’t have a spoiler when voters have multiple options,” said Joelle Hall, a longtime labor leader working against Ballot Measure 2.

But that argument got much more difficult to make after The New York Times reported a successful effort by Democrats to recruit a candidate named Dan Sullivan to appear on the ballot alongside Senator Dan Sullivan, the incumbent Republican whom Ms. Peltola, a former Democratic House member, hopes to defeat.

Besides Ms. Peltola and the two Sullivans, another name is on the ballot, Gerald Heikes, a conservative Republican and frequent candidate who said he too was recruited to run for the Senate by an outsider. A liberal political action committee is promoting Mr. Heikes in hopes of siphoning still more votes from the incumbent.

So two of the four choices may be on the ballot because of skulduggery.

Alaska Governor Mike Dunleavy, a conservative Republican leaving office in December, told Fox News this week that “we wouldn’t be having this conversation if we didn’t have ranked choice voting.”

Under current law, candidates for state and federal office in Alaska compete in one open, nonpartisan primary, with the top four advancing to November. Voters rank them in order of preference. If no candidate wins a majority of first-choice votes, the last-place finisher is eliminated and those votes are redistributed according to voters’ next choices. The process repeats until someone wins a majority of the remaining votes.

Ballot Measure 2 would return Alaska to primaries open only to voters registered to a particular party. That would be followed by a traditional general election where voters choose just one candidate. The initiative would also repeal campaign-finance disclosure requirements adopted with the current system. Proponents of the current system have made the loss of that transparency the heart of their argument to voters.

Even before the controversy over the two Dan Sullivans, the ballot measure was emerging as a proxy fight in a broader national battle over how America votes. Elon Musk, the world’s first trillionaire, and Jeff Yass, a billionaire, donated heavily to the repeal effort, while Michael Bloomberg, Marc Merrill and Kathryn Murdoch, themselves deep-pocketed donors, backed the campaign to keep the system.

The Times investigation has put proponents for the ranked-choice system in the awkward position of arguing that this kind of attempt to mislead could happen under any voting system because it’s comparatively easy for people to file to run in Alaska.

“This has nothing to do with ranked-choice voting,” said Scott Kendall, an Anchorage lawyer who designed the system. “It’s just a dirty trick.”

Ms. Peltola’s effort to unseat Senator Sullivan is critical to Democratic hopes of retaking the chamber. In response to the allegations of chicanery, Vice President JD Vance told reporters Thursday, “It seems to me that you have an election, the person who wins the most votes should win.”

President Trump said on a Kansas City radio broadcast, “You need about a 190 I.Q.” to understand the system,” though each ballot has fairly simple instructions and the state elections division, overseen by a Republican lieutenant governor, took pains to differentiate the candidates: Dan S. Sullivan is identified on the ballot as the incumbent and a registered Republican, while Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. has no identification next to his name.

Proponents of ranked-choice voting say it just gives voters more than one chance to decide who they support — and a simple solution, supporters note, to any confusion about which Dan is which: Rank them both.

Alaskans who rank Daniel J. Sullivan or Mr. Heikes first could still help Senator Dan S. Sullivan win, provided they also rank him ahead of Ms. Peltola. Only if they rank Ms. Peltola higher, or leave the incumbent off their ballots entirely, could the maneuver deprive him of votes he might otherwise receive.

Alaska Republicans have a history of refusing to rank their choices, and the senator’s latest radio ad features a catchy jingle encouraging people to rank “Dan S., Daniel, Gerry, just don’t rank Mary.”

“Republicans can be very stubborn,” Ms. Eledge said. “Some of them don’t like the system, so they don’t use it.”

That approach could be even more consequential in the race for governor, also on this year’s ballot.

A Democrat hasn’t won the job since 1998, but Democratic candidates finished first and second in the top-four August primary, which featured 17 candidates — 12 of them Republicans.

The second-place Democrat dropped out to clear a path for the other, a former state legislator, Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins. The top Republican finisher, Bernadette Wilson, urged the other two Republicans on the November ballot to do the same, but they refused. Earlier this month, President Trump backed Ms. Wilson and called on the other two Republicans to leave the race.

It all has some conservatives worried their voters will ignore repeated party instructions to “rank the red” and instead list only one candidate.

A similar approach helped Ms. Peltola defeat two Republicans, Sarah Palin and Nick Begich III, in a 2022 U.S. House race. The combined first-choice vote share for the two Republicans exceeded Ms. Peltola’s. But about a fifth of Mr. Begich’s voters only ranked him. When he fell out of the race, Ms. Peltola expanded her lead to win.

Polls have shown Mr. Kreiss-Tomkins leading the governors race, and he has promised to build a politically balanced cabinet and work closely with Republicans and independents in the legislature, which has been governed by a bipartisan coalition.

Proponents of the current system say its repeal could make such cooperation more difficult, by bringing back partisan primaries, which favor the extremes in both parties and gives Republican and Democratic leaders far more power to keep members focused on the party line.

That’s exactly what Ms. Eledge and other opponents of the current system want.

She’s eager, for example, to punish Senator Lisa Murkowski, a Republican, for her recent cross-party endorsement of Mr. Kreiss-Tomkins.

If Ballot Measure 2 passes, Ms. Eledge predicted, “she won’t run again.”

She added, “she knows she wouldn’t make it out of the primary.”

Of course, Ms. Murkowski could do what she did in 2010 when she lost the Republican primary to a hard-line conservative: launch a successful write-in campaign, without ranked-choice.

item.title: Federal Agency Emails Praising Trump May Violate Ethics Laws, Experts Say
item.description:
The Social Security Administration and the Internal Revenue Service praised President Trump in mass emails sent Thursday, Friday and Saturday to people with online accounts, an unusual move days before the midterm elections that some experts said could violate federal ethics laws.

“Under President Donald J. Trump, the Social Security Administration (SSA) is transforming into a model of excellence, one that meets and exceeds customer expectations for fast, accurate and secure service,” Frank Bisignano, the Social Security Agency’s commissioner, wrote in one of the emails, copies of which were reviewed by The New York Times.

Mr. Bisignano, who also serves as the chief executive of the I.R.S., signed his name on a similar email sent out by the I.R.S. on Thursday, copies of which were also reviewed by The Times.

“Last year, President Donald J. Trump signed into law the Working Families Tax Cuts, landmark legislation that ushered in a new era of tax relief and prevented the largest tax increase in American history from taking effect,” Mr. Bisignano wrote in the other email, continuing, “Hardworking Americans like you are keeping more of what they earn because of President Trump’s historic tax cuts.”

The I.R.S. email says that it is “for informational purposes and does not constitute a communication about a taxpayer’s specific situation,” adding that the I.R.S. “does not generally send e-mails to taxpayers.”

Several legal experts said the emails’ praise of Mr. Trump, coupled with their timing just days before a pivotal election, potentially violated the Hatch Act, an 87-year-old law meant to prevent employees of the executive branch from using their positions to influence the results of partisan elections.

Kathleen Clark, a law professor at Washington University in St. Louis, said the emails seemed to function as “propaganda” rather than as public service announcements providing practical information.

“They’re doing it just before the election to persuade people that President Trump is doing a good job,” Richard W. Painter, a law professor at the University of Minnesota and former White House ethics lawyer under President George W. Bush, said in a phone interview on Saturday, adding that he thought the emails were inappropriate.

Ms. Clark said the messages were reminiscent of a television ad campaign by the Trump administration this fall that promoted his presidency. Some experts said the campaign could have violated the Hatch Act and additional statutory prohibitions on the use of appropriated funds for publicity or propaganda.

The Social Security Administration and the I.R.S. did not respond to requests for comment.

item.title: Haley Stevens Abandons El-Sayed, Endorsing Mike Rogers in Michigan
item.description:
Representative Haley Stevens, Democrat of Michigan, on Sunday withdrew her support for Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for Senate in the state and her former primary rival, and endorsed his Republican opponent, a stunning last-minute turn in a race that is critical to the battle for Senate control.

“Our Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate, Abdul, said that I was no longer welcome in his campaign and that I should stay away,” Ms. Stevens said in a video on social media. “And he’s right. And that’s why I am endorsing Mike Rogers for the United States Senate.”

The extraordinary development reflected both the bitter disagreements over Israel and the personal animosity between the two prominent Michigan Democrats.

Ms. Stevens, a moderate and a strong supporter of Israel, often clashed with Dr. El-Sayed, an outspoken progressive critic of the country, during their contentious primary race. After he narrowly beat her in August, she immediately endorsed him and they seemed to reach a quiet truce. Then, this month, she began to criticize him in news interviews, and in recent days, they traded public barbs over his stance on Israel. But she continued to cautiously commit to supporting Dr. El-Sayed and the full Democratic ticket.

Ms. Stevens’s endorsement video went online while she appeared on Sunday morning with Mr. Rogers at a Black church in Detroit. In the video, she said she did not “belong in Abdul’s campaign,” nor did she “stand with” Hasan Piker, a provocative left-wing streamer with whom Dr. El-Sayed campaigned in the primary and from whom he later distanced himself.

Ms. Stevens cast the Senate race — which has also included waves of Republican attacks on Dr. El-Sayed’s Muslim faith and background — as a referendum on hate in politics. She added that she was “still a very proud Democrat.”

Miles away, Dr. El-Sayed was at a church service with other Democratic leaders, an event that had been intended to display party unity. On Saturday, he had publicly urged Ms. Stevens to stay away from that gathering, deepening the growing tension between the two Democrats.

After the news of Ms. Stevens’s endorsement of Mr. Rogers, Dr. El-Sayed sought to downplay its significance.

“None of this matters,” he told reporters.

Ms. Stevens’s move shocked other Democrats and upended her congressional office, with several top officials announcing their resignations. Many Democrats condemned the effort to undermine Dr. El-Sayed so close to an important election for the party.

item.title: Some Americans Are Fearful of Federal Interference on Election Day
item.description:
In the final hours before the midterm elections, some Americans say they are worried about federal interference in the vote and potential efforts by Republicans to overturn the results if the party is unsuccessful.

For years, President Trump has sowed doubts about the nation’s electoral system by promoting debunked claims of mail-ballot fraud, faulty voting machines and voting rolls riddled with noncitizens. As polls show the Republican majority in Congress in peril, Mr. Trump has ramped up his baseless attacks, even dangling a $1 million reward to tipsters who help secure a voting-fraud conviction.

Some voters are nervous about what he might do next.

“I am very concerned that the election will be disrupted in ways that will affect the margins,” said Tiffany Hall, a 56-year-old physician who lives in a suburb of Cincinnati.

Civil rights groups and labor unions recently sued the Trump administration, seeking to block the potential deployment of federal agents at the polls.

Ms. Hall, who is Black, voted early on Saturday with her husband and her teenage daughter, who was voting for the first time. Ms. Hall invoked the struggles of the civil rights movement and said she was worried about efforts to suppress the vote.

So is Jeanne Russell, a 77-year-old retiree and registered Democrat who lives in Verona Island, Maine. “I’m kind of foreseeing that there will be some dirty tricks,” she said.

But Ms. Russell added that she was optimistic that election officials were prepared to respond to any intervention by the federal government.

Nearly three-quarters of voters said they largely trusted that the results of Tuesday’s election would be accurate, including large majorities of Democrats, Republicans and independents, according to a recent New York Times/Siena poll.

But half of likely voters said that they were worried about the possibility that Republicans might try to overturn the outcome of the election. By comparison, 31 percent of voters said they were worried about Democrats doing the same.

Mike Massie, a 52-year-old teacher who recently voted in suburban Cincinnati, said he was not concerned about widespread voting irregularities. He recalled all the hoops he had to jump through recently after he moved and notified election officials about his new address.

“It would take some duplicity to try to cast a fraudulent vote,” said Mr. Massie, who described himself as a centrist who leans Republican. Asked if he was concerned about illegal voters, he said, “If there are any, I don’t think it’s enough to sway an election.”

Esther Bowling, 43, of Trenton, Ohio, is not so sure about that. She was a strong supporter of a Republican-backed measure in 2023 that required voters in her state to present a driver’s license, passport or other official photo ID to vote in person. Voters in Ohio will now consider a ballot measure to enshrine that requirement in the state constitution.

“If you are an American citizen you should have to show a photo ID to vote,” Ms. Bowling said.

Civil rights activists argue that such laws can disenfranchise Black people, younger and older voters, and those serving in the military and living abroad. Photo ID laws have gained traction in Republican-led states since Mr. Trump and his allies sought to overturn his defeat in the 2020 election.

In Georgia, some voters casting ballots this year recalled Mr. Trump’s phone call to Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger, urging him to “find” 11,780 votes.

Lasley Gober, 74, a retired Atlanta schoolteacher, said she was feeling uneasy about the midterm elections since January, when the F.B.I. seized ballots and other voting materials related to the 2020 election in Fulton County, Ga. The raid was part of an ongoing investigation by the Justice Department into the vote in the most populous county in Georgia.

“I’m a little scared about what they may try to do, to act like they won this,” Ms. Gober said.

Earlier this year, under pressure from voting rights groups, the Republican-controlled Georgia legislature abandoned a redistricting effort that would have erased U.S. House seats in majority-Black districts. That effort was weighing on Mary Hooks, a civil rights activist in Atlanta, as she considered the candidates on the 2026 ballot.

“They’re going to try to take the vote by hook or crook,” she said. “We’re going to see all manner of ways in which they’re going to continue to suppress the vote.”

Murray Carpenter contributed reporting from Maine and Sean Keenan from Atlanta.

item.title: Senator Chris Murphy Is ‘Awake and Alert’ After Suffering a Stroke
item.description:
Senator Christopher S. Murphy, Democrat of Connecticut, was hospitalized on Saturday after suffering a stroke, according to a statement from his chief of staff.

The chief of staff, Allison Herwitt, said that Mr. Murphy, 53, was attending his son’s hockey game on Saturday afternoon and “started experiencing numbness in his arm.” He was taken to a nearby hospital, where doctors diagnosed a stroke.

Mr. Murphy was transferred to Johns Hopkins Hospital in Baltimore for monitoring and treatment. “The doctors are encouraged by his progress; he is awake and alert; and we are optimistic he will make a full recovery,” Ms. Herwitt said in her statement.

A spokesman for Mr. Murphy would not provide further details about his condition on Sunday.

Mr. Murphy, who became a senator in 2013 and has been viewed as a potential 2028 presidential candidate, has spent the past several weeks on the campaign trail with Democrats as he tries to help his party take control of Congress in the midterm elections. He had been scheduled to help campaign in New Hampshire on Sunday.

Mr. Murphy is one of several senators to experience significant public health issues in recent years, as the health of politicians has received greater scrutiny. The sudden death of Senator Lindsey Graham, Republican of South Carolina, in July from an aortic dissection, a tear in the body’s main artery, added to those concerns.

At least two of Mr. Murphy’s colleagues have had strokes in recent years. Senator Chris Van Hollen, Democrat of Maryland, experienced what he said was a “minor stroke” in 2022. Senator John Fetterman, Democrat of Pennsylvania, had a near-fatal stroke that same year, as he was campaigning for election.

Senator Mitch McConnell, Republican of Kentucky and the former majority leader, was gone from the Capitol and out of public view for more than three months earlier this year after a health incident at his home.

Mr. McConnell has also appeared to experience medical issues at the Capitol and in Kentucky, freezing during appearances and needing to be escorted away by his aides.

item.title: Why The Times Doesn’t Rely on Exit Polls
item.description:
Exit polls — surveys of voters taken immediately after they exit their polling stations — have long been a hallmark of election coverage. Now they rely heavily on pre-election polling. While exit polls are popular on TV and social media, The Times does not generally rely on them in our reporting of the election.

The primary reason is that exit polls, in general, have a poor track record. They have contributed to misleading narratives on election night, including in 2016 when exit polls of the presidential race showed Hillary Clinton ahead of Donald J. Trump. Later, they showed a majority of white women voting for Mr. Trump. Both of those things proved to be untrue.

Our search for a better way to know as much about an election as possible led to the creation of Times Voter Trends, a project that will break down estimates for the results of U.S. House and Senate elections by age, race, education and gender in every state in the country. We will report our preliminary findings late on election night, and will update them as more data arrives.

To make this project as authoritative as possible, we will attempt to recontact the roughly 30,000 people we interviewed this year for Times/Siena polls to verify whether they voted and for whom. We will combine that information with actual election results at the precinct and county level, and estimates from our election night live model, The Needle, into a comprehensive analysis of what happened in the election.

To get readers started, we have retroactively released our findings from the 2024 and 2020 elections.

item.title: Judge Rejects Trump Officials’ Move to Challenge Alaska Senate Election
item.description:
A federal judge in Alaska has dismissed the Trump administration’s lawsuit that pre-emptively challenged the results in a U.S. Senate race featuring two candidates with the same name — a Republican incumbent and another man who could be a spoiler.

The ruling is the latest in a series of court defeats for the Trump administration, which has been seeking to intervene in state-administered elections.

On Friday, the U.S. District Court in California blocked the administration from threatening to prosecute state and local election officials who do not comply with the department’s directives on handling ballots.

Also on Friday, a federal appeals court panel denied a request to order California officials to set aside about 20,000 mail-in ballots that the administration claimed had been sent to possible noncitizens.

In Alaska, the Justice Department filed its lawsuit last month at President Trump’s direction, asking the judge to block certification of the state’s U.S. Senate election results if Senator Daniel S. Sullivan loses but would have won had votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan, a retired teacher, gone to the incumbent instead.

In that scenario, the suit also demands an investigation into whether voters who selected the retired teacher actually intended to vote for the senator.

Federal officials have not made clear how an investigation into anonymous ballots would be conducted.

In her Sunday ruling, Chief Judge Sharon Gleason of U.S. District Court in Alaska wrote that she did not see how the federal government’s proposed solution to any confusion would solve the problem if it even existed — or how the approach could work given the right to a secret ballot is a core principle of American democracy.

The federal government, she wrote, “offers no rebuttal to the concerns regarding preservation of the secrecy of voting and provides no explanation of how its request for ballot segregation and a court-ordered investigation by law enforcement officers into certain voters’ intent could be implemented while preserving the secrecy of the ballot.”

Kiersten Pels, a spokeswoman for the Department of Justice, said the administration plans to appeal the dismissal and noted that the judge didn’t not address “the argument of the United States that Daniel J. Sullivan (a/k/a Decoy Dan) entered the race as a frivolous candidate to confuse voters.”

The administration’s lawsuit accuses Daniel J. Sulivan of trying to “dupe Alaska’s voters into believing that he is Senator Sullivan.” Daniel J. Sullivan has said he voted for Democrats in the last three presidential races and for Mary Peltola, the current Democratic Senate nominee on the ballot, in her 2022 and 2024 campaigns for Congress.

The suit also notes that he switched his party affiliation from Independent to Republican only when he filed to run, and that his campaign website uses the same dark blue and yellow color scheme as the incumbent’s.

A New York Times investigation revealed that a Democratic operative connected to Ms. Peltola’s campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee enlisted Daniel J. Sullivan to run as part of a broader effort to recruit independent and third-party candidates who might peel votes away from the incumbent.

Gov. Mike Dunleavy, a Republican, has ordered a criminal investigation into the Peltola campaign even as the state elections division, overseen by his lieutenant governor, also a Republican, fought the Trump administration’s civil lawsuit.

Ms. Peltola and national Democrats have denied any connection to Daniel J. Sullivan’s candidacy, and they joined the civil case as additional defendants along with national Democrats, the League of Women Voters and Common Cause, a self-described nonpartisan government watchdog organization.

Daniel S. Sullivan, the incumbent senator, promised in an interview with CNN Sunday to support any election results but also suggested, without offering explanation or details, that the election could be “stolen.”

In its defense in the Justice Department’s lawsuit, lawyers with the state of Alaska noted that state courts had already rejected an attempt by the state’s elections agency to take Daniel J. Sullivan off the ballot and that the final ballot was designed to differentiate between the two men: It lists the senator as “Dan S. Sullivan” and notes his party affiliation and incumbency, and the other man is “Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.” with no party affiliation included.

Alaska also uses ranked choice voting in state and federal general elections, meaning voters are familiar with the system. Any voter confused by the existence of two Dan Sullivans could simply rank both candidates.

Judge Gleason had already expressed skepticism of the Trump administration’s case in a ruling last month agreeing to a speedy hearing. In that order, she pointed out that the federal lawsuit came after Alaskans had already begun casting ballots for November and nearly four months after the Alaska Supreme Court directed the state Division of Elections to include Daniel J. Sullivan on the ballot.

In Sunday’s dismissal ruling, she noted that federal lawyers, in their filings, said they were not attempting to interfere in the time, place and manner of Alaskan elections — matters the U.S. Constitution leaves in the hands of states.

But, Judge Gleason said, the federal government’s proposed answers to any voter confusion were “a court order preventing the State from certifying the election if certain circumstances occur; a court order requiring the State to segregate and preserve certain ballots; and a court order permitting the United States to conduct an investigation into the intent of those voters who cast ballots for Daniel J. Sullivan.

“These requests certainly involve the time, place, and manner of Alaska’s election,” she wrote.

If anything, the judge added, such federal intervention amid an ongoing election would cause the precise sort of voter confusion the administration says it is trying to prevent.

Bayliss Wagner and Glenn Thrush contributed reporting.

item.title: A Desperate Mayday as Small Jet Plummets to Ground in Florida, Killing 9
item.description:
The pilot of a midsize business jet carrying nine people from Texas to Florida desperately declared a mayday as the plane rapidly lost altitude and plummeted to the ground nose-first before exploding into a fireball, killing all on board.

The plane, a Learjet 60, had departed Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas and was headed to North Eleuthera Airport in the Bahamas, the Federal Aviation Administration said.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, in a separate statement, confirmed that those aboard had died.

There was no information available about the identities of those on the plane or whether anyone on the ground was injured.

Photos and video posted online showed a small plane plunging nose first into the ground and exploding. Footage showed the plane crashing near a busy thoroughfare close to traffic, and leaving a fiery crater in the roadway.

Just before the plane crashed, a pilot radioed air traffic controllers that the plane was facing rain and “light, clear ice that is manageable and moderate turbulence,” according to archived communications between the pilot and air traffic controllers in Miami on Sunday afternoon.

The pilot asked if she could climb to 37,000 feet, but soon after, she desperately declared mayday, a life-threatening emergency, to air traffic controllers.

She screamed that the plane was “descending 20,000 feet per minute.”

“We’re going to crash into the ground,” she said before shrieking, “We’re going to die!”

For several minutes after that, air traffic controllers tried unsuccessfully to communicate with the plane.

The plane crashed just outside the boundaries of the City of Greenacres in unincorporated Palm Beach County, according to Austin Lee, a city spokesman. Greenacres is about four miles west of Palm Springs.

It was not immediately clear what led up to the crash.

The F.A.A. and National Transportation Safety Board said Sunday that they were investigating the crash.

Johnny Diaz contributed reporting.

item.title: Kansas Senator Goes Rogue With Video Response to Medical Debt Lawsuits
item.description:
About two weeks ago, Senator Roger Marshall of Kansas, an embattled Republican, approached the senior leadership of his campaign with an idea.

Mr. Marshall, an obstetrician facing re-election, wanted to film an ad responding to all of the attacks he was taking on medical debts.

Back when he was a full-time doctor, Mr. Marshall filed lawsuits against more than 700 patients, seeking payments of their debts, and at least 81 were arrested when the patients missed court dates, The New York Times reported in September. Others faced wage garnishments. Mr. Marshall routinely charged an 18 percent interest rate on the outstanding debts.

The litigation — and its fallout — has become a central campaign issue.

Mr. Marshall wanted to personally push back, according to four people with knowledge of the matter, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe internal deliberations ahead of the election.

His top advisers said no. Such an ad was a bad idea so close to the election, they argued, and Mr. Marshall needed to contrast his record with Adam Hamilton, his Democratic rival, especially on immigration.

That’s when Mr. Marshall went rogue.

The senator — without the knowledge of at least some top aides — arranged for his own film crew to record and package just such an ad.

Wearing a red button-down shirt in front of a bucolic background, Mr. Marshall made the case in a 60-second ad that he had often provided free care.

“We did have to keep the lights on,” Mr. Marshall said. “So we occasionally handed some accounts over to a collection agency, just like nearly every private medical practice does.”

“My involvement in any patient’s account ended the minute it was turned over to an outside agency,” he went on. “I never had anyone arrested.”

Mr. Marshall sent a copy of the would-be ad to other aides on the campaign and asked that it be part of a paid advertising program, according to two of the people.

Top campaign leaders moved to block the release of the ad, believing it would do more harm than good.

Mr. Marshall, however, did not give up. He began sending it directly to people outside the campaign, according to the two people, who were briefed on Mr. Marshall’s texts.

On Saturday evening, Pete Mundo, a Kansas City talk radio host, posted the video on X, which is how it became public.

Mr. Mundo did not immediately respond to an email about how he obtained the video.

The written disclaimer at the end of the video says: “Paid for By Kansans for Marshall. Approved by Roger Marshall.”

The Marshall campaign declined to discuss the origin story of the video.

“If the best that our haters have is a video that the campaign hasn’t posted or isn’t running anywhere as an ad and that only Twitter is talking about goes to show you that Senator Marshall is on track for a great night on November 3rd,” said Alex DeGrasse, a campaign spokesman.

Mr. Marshall’s pursuit of medical debts has been featured prominently in Democratic commercials. One from the Hamilton campaign featured a woman describing the day the police came to arrest her while she was eight months pregnant and home with her 2-year-old daughter.

Mr. Marshall’s medical practice had sued her in 2009 for $3,596 in outstanding debt for a C-section delivery. Over six years, she was arrested three times for missing court dates related to the case.

One of Mr. Marshall’s former lawyers, who handled many of his debt collection cases, previously told The Times that Mr. Marshall had decided which cases to send to his firm but did not weigh in on what steps the firm took in court, nor did he set any limits on how far it could go to collect. That lawyer, Steven Johnson, also said that it was Mr. Marshall’s office that set an 18 percent interest rate on the debts.

Mr. Marshall sent the Hamilton campaign a cease-and-desist letter regarding his advertisement featuring the former patient, calling it “defamatory.” The Hamilton campaign has defended the ad and has continued to run it on local television.

Emily Davies contributed reporting.

item.title: Haley Stevens Bashed Mike Rogers Until She Endorsed Him
item.description:
Representative Haley Stevens, Democrat of Michigan, was one of the fiercest critics of the Republican Mike Rogers, a former congressman, in the state’s Senate race until her striking reversal on Sunday.

Ms. Stevens, who smiled next to Mr. Rogers at a Detroit church as a video announcing she had endorsed him was posted on social media, once pitched herself to Democratic voters as their best chance of stopping Mr. Rogers. She pilloried him for his stance on issues as various as health care, trade, the environment, abortion, election integrity and foreign policy. Ms. Stevens twice voted to impeach President Trump and frequently cast Mr. Rogers as one of his eager acolytes.

She narrowly lost the Democratic primary to Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, whom she initially endorsed after her loss. She still regularly criticized Mr. Rogers as recently as August, when she said, among other things, that he “will be another rubber stamp for Donald Trump’s dangerous agenda.”

As Ms. Stevens and Dr. El-Sayed publicly feuded in recent weeks over U.S. policy on Israel, their relationship deteriorated, leading to her defection to Mr. Rogers. Her decision led several of her staff members to resign and incensed Democrats nationwide, who feared her endorsement could put a key Senate seat at risk.

Before her reversal, here are some of the harshest critiques Ms. Stevens lobbed at Mr. Rogers over the course of the campaign:

“Mike Rogers’ record on LGBTQ+ rights is repulsive. He has no business representing Michiganders.” (June 2026)

item.title: Halloween Shootings Leave at Least 24 Dead and 94 Wounded Nationwide
item.description:
Three shootings early on the morning of Nov. 1 left at least four dead and 15 injured in the Deep Ellum neighborhood of Dallas, Texas, officials confirmed on Sunday.

The hail of Texas gunfire was part of a wave of violence on Halloween that left at least 24 dead and 94 wounded across the country, according to police statements. The shootings stretched from California to Delaware. They unfolded at night clubs, costume stores, outside stadiums and near college campuses.

The violence came as the nation celebrated Halloween, a holiday that mixes costume-clad revelers with alcohol consumption and drug use. Those ingredients, coupled with access to firearms, can lead to violence, experts say.

It is unknown whether this weekend’s violence was outsized for recent holiday weekends, but previous studies have shown spikes in violence on Halloween.

For instance, Oct. 31 ranks as the third-most violent day of the year, following only July 4 and Jan. 1, according to an analysis of F.B.I. incident data for Boston from 2005 to 2009 by James Alan Fox, a criminologist at Northeastern University.

For minors, Oct. 31 is the most dangerous day of the year, he added.

“They are out in the evening, interacting with strangers,” Dr. Fox said in an interview on Sunday.

In Detroit, a 5-year-old still in her Halloween costume was struck in her chest by a bullet as she played in the backroom of her house after a night of trick-or-treating, Arnold Williams, the deputy chief of the Detroit Police Department, said at a news briefing.

“She had to tell her mom, ‘I think I’ve been shot,’” he said. The 5-year-old is in stable condition.

In Jacksonville, Fla., 13 people were shot and two died in two unrelated shootings.

While waiting in line for a Halloween party, a 17-year-old girl was killed by a stray bullet at around 1:40 a.m. on Sunday. Two others injured in that incident had also been “unintended targets,” according to the Jacksonville Police Department.

At another location in Jacksonville, 10 people were shot at around 3:45 a.m. on Sunday as a house party of more than 100 people spilled into the street. A 20-year-old man was killed, and a 15-year-old girl was injured but in stable condition. One victim remains in critical condition.

A shooting also occurred at a nightclub in Jackson, Miss., which left two dead and four injured.

At a costume store in Northern California, a gunman killed a pregnant mother of four and injured six others, including two teenagers who were in critical condition on Saturday.

In Oklahoma City, officers responded to a disturbance at a trailer park during a Halloween party. One person suffered multiple gunshot wounds to the leg and is expected to survive. Two people at the scene were fatally struck by a vehicle, but the exact circumstances were unclear, according to the Oklahoma City Police Department.

More than two dozen people were shot near college campuses or at university events.

One person was killed and eight people were injured outside Legion Field in Birmingham, Ala., where Alabama A&M played Alabama State earlier in the day, in a rivalry matchup known as the Magic City Classic.

About 600 miles north, in Bloomington, Ill., officers assisted eight gunshot victims near the Illinois Wesleyan University campus. A 19-year-old woman was pronounced dead at the scene. Seven others were transported to area hospitals, and one of them remains in critical condition, according to the Bloomington Police Department.

As officers responded in Illinois, local police in Bloomington, Ind., about 200 miles southeast, heard gunfire erupt from a large crowd near the campus of Indiana University, which was celebrating homecoming in addition to Halloween.

“Multiple individuals were located in the downtown area with wounds believed to have been caused by the shooting,” the Bloomington Police Department said in a statement.

Seven people were transported to area hospitals. Officers detained a male subject who fled the area with an exposed firearm, but they said they did not know if he had discharged the weapon.

Even as the data points to the risk of violence on Halloween, preventing it is difficult, experts on gun violence say.

“The police can’t be inside every bar. They can’t be in every parking lot,” said Alexis Piquero, a criminologist at the University of Miami and the former director of the Bureau of Justice Statistics in the Justice Department during the Biden administration.

In Dallas, at least four people were killed and 15 others were injured in the three shootings in the Deep Ellum neighborhood, which occurred within about a 75-minute period. There was no indication that the shootings were connected, and the number of casualties could continue to rise, the authorities said.

“We knew it was Saturday night. We knew it was Halloween, so we were staffed properly,” Daniel Comeaux, the Dallas police chief, said at news briefing on Sunday.

Images and videos circulating on social media showed people running for safety in the streets of Deep Ellum, which is home to several bars, restaurants and concert venues. Recently, the neighborhood has been plagued by safety concerns over of a wave of crime . At least seven bars and restaurants, including some longtime establishments, have closed in Deep Ellum this year.

By Sunday morning, the streets were largely empty and littered with trash after police cordoned off parts of the neighborhood.

“This is completely unacceptable,” Chief Comeaux said.

item.title: Democrats Show Strength in Final Days of Race for the Senate, New Polls Find
item.description:
Democrats are ahead of Republicans in almost all of the seven battleground states that will determine which party controls the Senate, according to the final set of polls from The New York Times and Siena University before the midterm elections.

The surveys found that Democrats hold sizable leads in Texas, which has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1988, and Kansas, which has not elected one since 1932.

To win a Senate majority, Democrats need to defend all the seats they currently hold and flip at least four seats that are currently held by Republicans. It has been seen as an uphill battle because many of the seats they need to win are in Republican strongholds.

But the new polls found Democratic candidates ahead in five states that now have Republican senators and effectively tied in a sixth. They hold leads in Kansas, Maine, Ohio and Texas and a narrow edge in Alaska. They are effectively tied in Iowa.

In Michigan, the lone top Senate battleground already held by Democrats, the poll found the Democratic candidate leading by double digits. (It was conducted before a Democratic feud erupted in Michigan this weekend.) The surveys did not include North Carolina, where polls have long found the Democrat leading and Republicans have pared back their campaign spending.

Dissatisfaction with President Trump and frustration over his management of the economy are dragging down Republicans, according to the polls. Just 38 percent of likely voters approved of the president’s job performance in the seven states in the poll, a strikingly low figure given that Mr. Trump had won five of the states by double digits just two years ago.

The newfound Democratic strength was powered by growing trust in the party to handle the economy — the key motivating issue for voters this year. Democrats hold a nine-point advantage on the cost of living across the battlegrounds, and they led on this crucial measure in every single state.

If the polls are accurate and these trends hold, Democrats would win control of the Senate.

But there were some reasons for Democratic concern: There are still some undecided voters, and voters who decided only in the last month favored Republicans by a nine-point margin.

In the Senate race in Texas, James Talarico, a Democratic state legislator, held a seven-point edge over Ken Paxton, the Republican state attorney general, 50 percent to 43 percent among likely voters. Mr. Paxton had the worst image of any candidate included in the survey — by far.

In Maine, Senator Susan Collins, the last remaining Republican senator in New England, is trailing in her re-election campaign behind Troy Jackson, a Democratic former state senator. Mr. Jackson leads 51 percent to 45 percent among likely voters.

Polls are imperfect. Six years ago, Ms. Collins had trailed in every survey before the election — and she still won re-election comfortably.

But the new polls revealed a series of flashing warning signs for Republicans — about both their candidates and the broader political environment.

In every state but Maine, the Democratic Senate candidate was viewed more favorably than the Republican candidate.

And likely voters were unhappy with the leadership of Mr. Trump across the board, and said that they believed Democrats would do a better job handling the cost of living and foreign wars and doing what is best for ordinary people.

The New York Times/Siena poll

Oct. 23-Nov. 1

Based on New York Times/Siena polls of 610 voters in Alaska, 705 voters in Iowa, 736 voters in Kansas, 714 voters in Maine, 1,011 voters in Michigan, 717 voters in Ohio and 1,215 voters in Texas. Net favorability is the share of respondents who view the candidate favorably minus the share who view the candidate unfavorably.

Jillian Vordick/The New York Times

Mr. Trump has been barnstorming Republican states in a bid to re-energize his base in the final weeks before Election Day, but the polls suggest that enthusiasm for the president is slipping even within his party. In Ohio, where 82 percent of Republicans approve of the president, the share who approve “strongly” has fallen to 51 percent, down from 63 percent in June.

And in a Times/Siena poll last week, the Senate race was tied in heavily Republican South Carolina.

One key advantage for Democratic candidates is that they are leading with independent voters in every state surveyed. That includes Iowa, where Josh Turek, a Democratic state legislator, was effectively tied with Representative Ashley Hinson, the Republican nominee.

The polls found that the Democratic resurgence was powered by a renewed strength among younger voters and Latinos, as well as the relative weakness Republicans have among the party’s base of white, working-class voters.

Mr. Trump had made gains among Latino and younger voters in 2024. But this year, his party’s Senate candidates were winning only about one-quarter of younger voters and Latino voters.

Crumbling trust in Republicans on the economy — and in Mr. Trump in particular — helps to explain how Democrats are competitive in a state like Kansas. Mr. Trump won Kansas by the widest margin of any of the seven states polled, and the state has not elected a Democratic senator for nearly a century. But diesel prices that rose after the Iran war, and the administration’s decision to drop import tariffs on foreign beef, have dismayed farmers.

Adam Hamilton, the Democratic nominee and the pastor of the largest church in the state, leads Senator Roger Marshall, the Republican incumbent, 49 percent to 44 percent.

Mr. Hamilton also the support of 13 percent of Republicans, including James Gerety, 52, a retired National Guardsman living in Meriden, Kan., who said that he saw Mr. Hamilton as “a lot more genuine” than Mr. Marshall.

“I had reservations at first, with him being a pastor,” said Mr. Gerety, a registered Republican who considers himself more of an independent. “I get squirrelly with religion being brought into politics. But Hamilton is trying to lower prices, to get us out of this war with Iran. He’s trying to bring inflation down.”

Mr. Marshall has also faced criticism after The New York Times reported that he sued patients for unpaid medical debt, leading to arrests in some cases.

The Times previously polled all seven states in September. The Democrats improved in six of the states in the final poll (Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Ohio and Texas) and lost ground in only one (Alaska).

White working-class voters have been the backbone of Mr. Trump’s coalition. In 2024, he won an estimated 74 percent of white voters without college degrees, according to exit polls. Now, in these seven states, Republicans were winning just 56 percent of these voters.

Blue-collar white voters have proved particularly hard to reach in polls, and polling error has previously been among the highest in that demographic, a large group in all seven states.

Based on New York Times/Siena and New York Times/Portland Press Herald/Siena polls of likely voters conducted June 19 to 26, Sept. 15 to 22, Sept. 21 to Oct. 1 and Oct. 23 to Nov. 1. Margins are calculated using candidates’ unrounded vote shares.

Jillian Vordick/The New York Times

In Michigan, the lone Senate seat in the survey currently held by a Democrat, the poll showed Dr. Abdul El-Sayed ahead by a wide 11 percentage points over Mike Rogers, a Republican former congressman, who narrowly lost a Senate run in 2024.

Dr. El-Sayed, who has relished political combat in a way few other Democrats do, has performed especially well with men, a group that historically tilts Republican. He is running roughly even with the group, an improvement from September.

But in the Democratic primary, polls overestimated Dr. El-Sayed’s strength. And he has been embroiled in a bitter public feud with his primary rival, Representative Haley Stevens, who endorsed Mr. Rogers on Sunday in a rare cross-partisan embrace that has given Republicans hope. Still, Dr. El-Sayed is ahead by a wide margin on every issue in the poll, including immigration, a traditional Republican strength.

In Ohio, former Senator Sherrod Brown, a Democrat, leads Senator Jon Husted, a Republican, 49 percent to 44 percent in a race that has drawn half a billion dollars in spending, with Republicans spending $80 million more on ads, according to AdImpact, the ad-tracking service.

The New York Times/Siena Poll

Oct. 23-Nov. 1

Based on New York Times/Siena polls of 610 voters in Alaska, 705 voters in Iowa, 736 voters in Kansas, 714 voters in Maine, 1,011 voters in Michigan, 717 voters in Ohio and 1,215 voters in Texas. Question wording has been condensed.

Jillian Vordick/The New York Times

In Maine, Mr. Jackson, the Democratic challenger, has improved his image since September, though he is still seen unfavorably overall. Critically, he is running in the most Democratic state on the battleground map, and he remains much more popular than Mr. Trump.

In Texas, 49 percent of likely voters view Mr. Talarico favorably, while 39 percent view him unfavorably, giving him a 10-point-edge on favorability despite an enormous, very negative ad campaign against him funded chiefly by Elon Musk, the world’s richest person.

Mr. Paxton, Mr. Talarico’s G.O.P. opponent, has seen his image decline in recent months. Fifty-four percent of likely voters there now view him unfavorably, while only 33 percent view him favorably.

Rey Gonzales, a 62-year-old Republican living in Houston, said that he had been troubled by the allegations that led to Mr. Paxton’s impeachment and by reports that he had been unfaithful in his marriage. Mr. Gonzales, who says he voted for Mr. Trump in 2016 and 2020 but did not vote in 2024, says he plans to support Mr. Talarico purely out of dislike for Mr. Paxton.

When asked what he liked about Mr. Talarico, his answer was succinct: “Nothing.”

In Alaska, Mary Peltola, the former Democratic congresswoman challenging Senator Dan Sullivan, has faced criticism after a New York Times investigation found political operatives aligned with her recruited another candidate, Dan J. Sullivan, to run as a Republican in the race to try to pull votes away from the Republican incumbent.

The poll was mostly completed before the release of the story. Even so, Ms. Peltola was the only Democrat in this set of polls to lose ground since an earlier Times/Siena poll. The poll found her with a narrow edge over Mr. Sullivan, 48 percent to 46 percent.

Sophia June contributed reporting.

Here are the key things to know about these New York Times/Siena polls:

Interviewers spoke with 610 voters in Alaska, 705 voters in Iowa, 714 voters in Maine, 717 voters in Ohio, 736 voters in Kansas, 1,011 voters in Michigan, and 1,215 voters in Texas from Oct. 23 to Nov. 1, 2026.

You can see full results and a detailed methodology here. If you want to read more about how and why we conduct our polls, you can see answers to frequently asked questions and submit your own questions here.

item.title: What to Know About the Florida Plane Crash That Killed 9
item.description:
The authorities are continuing to investigate how a plane carrying nine people on Sunday afternoon climbed to an altitude of 37,000 feet, then suddenly fell from the sky at a rate of 20,000 feet per minute into a roadway outside Palm Beach, Fla.

All those on board were killed, the authorities said.

The Learjet 60 flight was traveling from Austin, Texas, to North Eleuthera Airport in the Bahamas.

The authorities have not released the identities of those on the plane.

“This was a cataclysmic plane crash,” Gov. Ron DeSantis of Florida said at a news conference on Sunday. “It looked like a missile going down.”

Here’s what we know.

Radio traffic between the pilot and air traffic control in Miami indicated that the plane was encountering “light, clear ice that is manageable and moderate turbulence,” on Sunday afternoon.

The pilot asked if she could climb to 37,000 feet, presumably to fly above the turbulent air. But moments later, she declared mayday, a life-threatening emergency, to traffic controllers.

The plane was “descending 20,000 feet per minute,” she screamed.

“We’re going to crash into the ground,” she added, before shrieking, “We’re going to die!”

The Federal Aviation Administration and the National Transportation Safety Board said they would be investigating the accident.

Local officials said on Sunday that they were evacuating about 600 residents in the small community of trailer homes near the impact zone, where smoldering chunks of metal ignited small fires throughout the community.

Officials said that no one on the ground was injured.

A cause for the crash was not immediately clear.

Aviation safety experts said that they were struck by the plane’s rapid loss of altitude and the mention of ice by the pilot.

The pilot was indicating that the “plane was uncontrollable,” Steven Arroyo, a retired United Airways airline captain said after listening to an audio recording of the conversation between air traffic controllers and the plane’s pilot.

Mary Schiavo, an aviation lawyer and former inspector general for the Department of Transportation, said that if too much ice builds up on the wings of a plane, it can destroy airflow, which could be consistent with how the plane turned and fell.

“That is a plane not descending, but a plane falling,” said Ms. Schiavo, who reviewed videos posted on social media and flight data. She added, “Icing can be so severe it can overcome and stall the plane.”

Esteban Ruiz, a resident of the trailer home community near where the crash occurred, said he was relaxing when he heard a loud noise and what he thought was rain pelting his roof. It was actually pieces of metal debris raining down from the plane’s impact. He said he rushed outside and saw chaos.

“I thought maybe it was lightning,” he said in Spanish of the crater in the ground from where the plane crashed.

Stephanie Platts, another resident of the community near the crash site, said that she was sitting on her patio with her family when she heard a loud noise that sounded like a car crash. Ms. Platts said she froze as her mobile home caught on fire, caused by flying debris from the plane hitting the ground.

Neighbors tried to help her put out the flames. She remembered seeing human remains scattered around her. And in the aftermath, she lost her dog named Moose, who ran away when the plane crashed. She hopes he took shelter somewhere in the midst of the chaos.

“Everything was engulfed in flames,” she said, “and then after the flames, was like rain of metal.”
